overview.text: Mahsa (Jina or Zhina) Amini was a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman whose death in September 2022 became a catalyst for protests across Iran. Tehran’s morality police arrested her on September 13 over an alleged violation of compulsory hijab rules. She fell into a coma and died in a hospital on September 16. Her death brought demands for accountability together with broader calls for women’s rights and political freedom. Protesters used the slogan “Woman, Life, Freedom,” and authorities responded with a violent crackdown. A United Nations fact-finding mission later concluded that the Iranian state bore responsibility for her unlawful death.

key_facts.text: Amini was arrested in Tehran on September 13, 2022, over an alleged hijab violation.
She died in a hospital on September 16 after falling into a coma following her arrest.
Her Kurdish name is commonly rendered Jina or Zhina.
The protests after her death became known as the Woman, Life, Freedom movement.

overview.text: The Cod Wars were a series of fishing-rights disputes between Iceland and the United Kingdom in the North Atlantic. The principal confrontations followed Icelandic extensions of its fishing limits in 1958, 1972–73, and 1975–76, ultimately to 200 nautical miles. British trawlers wanted continued access to waters around Iceland, while Iceland defended a fishing industry central to its economy. At sea, Icelandic coast-guard vessels cut trawler nets or cables, and British ships escorted the trawlers; vessels also collided. Agreements ended the successive disputes, with Britain eventually accepting Iceland’s wider fishing zone. The term “wars” describes tense maritime confrontations, not conventional land campaigns.

key_facts.text: The principal Cod Wars began after Icelandic fishing-limit extensions in 1958, 1972, and 1975.
Iceland’s claimed fishing limit reached 200 nautical miles in 1975.
Icelandic coast-guard crews used trawl-wire cutters against foreign fishing gear.
The final agreement was signed in June 1976.

overview.text: Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington, was a British soldier and statesman born in Dublin in 1769. His campaigns against Napoleon’s forces in Portugal and Spain during the Peninsular War established his military reputation and earned him the dukedom in 1814. When Napoleon returned to power, Wellington commanded a multinational allied army in the Netherlands. On June 18, 1815, his troops fought the French at Waterloo, where the arrival of Prussian forces under Gebhard von Blücher helped secure Napoleon’s defeat. Wellington later entered government and served as British prime minister. His career therefore spans both battlefield command and nineteenth-century politics.

key_facts.text: Arthur Wellesley was born in Dublin in 1769.
He was made Duke of Wellington in 1814 after the Peninsular War.
Waterloo was fought on June 18, 1815.
Prussian troops under Blücher helped Wellington’s multinational army defeat Napoleon.
Wellington later served as British prime minister.

overview.text: Trans-Saharan trade linked communities in West Africa with North Africa and the wider Mediterranean world through a network of desert caravan routes. From the early medieval period, camel caravans carried West African gold northward, while salt and other goods moved along the routes in several directions. Soninke Ghana and, later, Mali were important political centers connected to this exchange. Trade depended on African merchants, guides, miners, and towns across the Sahara and Sahel, rather than a single road or a simple gold-for-salt swap. Goods, people, religious practices, and ideas circulated through these connections, placing West Africa within a broad medieval economy.

key_facts.text: Camel caravans crossed the Sahara along multiple routes from the early medieval period.
Gold from West Africa supplied demand for coinage around the Mediterranean.
Saharan salt was one important commodity moving toward West African markets.
The Ghana and Mali states were connected to changing gold-trade routes.
Exchange also moved people, objects, and ideas between regions.

overview.text: The Battle of the Camel was an early conflict within the Muslim community, fought near Basra in 656 CE after the killing of Caliph Uthman. Ali, who became caliph after Uthman’s death, faced a coalition associated with Aisha, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, and the prominent companions Talha and al-Zubayr. The coalition demanded action over Uthman’s murder; political grievances also shaped the confrontation. Ali gathered support in Kufa, and attempts to negotiate failed before his forces won the battle. Its name refers to Aisha’s presence on a camel at the center of the fighting. The event became part of the First Fitna, a period of Muslim civil conflict.

key_facts.text: The battle took place near Basra in 656 CE.
Ali had become caliph after Uthman was killed.
Aisha, Talha, and al-Zubayr were associated with the opposing coalition.
The coalition demanded that Uthman’s killers be brought to trial.
The battle’s name refers to Aisha’s camel on the battlefield.

overview.text: Shona refers to related Bantu-speaking communities, primarily in present-day Zimbabwe, whose languages and local histories are diverse. Their heritage includes Great Zimbabwe, a major stone-built center that flourished between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries in the region. Its walls, pottery, and imported objects attest to skilled building, farming, and long-distance exchange. Later states in the area included Mutapa, but Shona communities were never one unchanging kingdom. Their history also lives in local places and practices: Shona communities in Buhera, for example, celebrate the Matendera stone site through music, food, and dance. Modern community perspectives help explain heritage beyond the ruins alone.

key_facts.text: “Shona” covers related communities and language varieties, not a single uniform culture.
Great Zimbabwe was built and occupied chiefly between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries.
Its Hill Ruins, Great Enclosure, and Valley Ruins are distinct parts of the site.
Excavations found evidence of exchange, including imported glass beads and porcelain.
Buhera communities celebrate Matendera’s Shona heritage through a local festival.

overview.text: The Potsdam Conference brought the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain together near Berlin from July 17 to August 2, 1945, after Germany’s defeat in World War II. Harry Truman and Joseph Stalin met with Winston Churchill, who was replaced during the conference by Clement Attlee after Britain’s election. The Allies discussed occupation and political reconstruction of Germany, reparations, borders, and the still-ongoing war against Japan. Their published agreement called for eliminating German militarism and Nazism and for joint administration through occupation authorities. Potsdam revealed both continued wartime cooperation and disagreements that would shape postwar Europe.

key_facts.text: The conference met near Potsdam from July 17 to August 2, 1945.
Truman and Stalin attended; Churchill was replaced by Attlee during the meeting.
Allied occupation and administration of Germany were central subjects.
The published agreement called for demilitarization and destruction of Nazi institutions.
The leaders also discussed the ongoing war with Japan.

overview.text: Bloody Sunday in Dublin on November 21, 1920, was a day of killings during the Irish War of Independence. In the morning, an Irish Republican Army unit struck people it identified as British intelligence personnel. That afternoon, British security forces entered Croke Park during a Dublin–Tipperary Gaelic football match and fired into the crowd. Fourteen people died at the stadium, including Tipperary player Michael Hogan, and many others were injured. Three more people held at Dublin Castle died that evening. The name often refers especially to the Croke Park shooting, but the wider sequence of violence gives the day its historical setting.

key_facts.text: Bloody Sunday in Dublin occurred on November 21, 1920.
The morning IRA operation targeted suspected British intelligence personnel.
The afternoon shooting occurred during a Dublin–Tipperary match at Croke Park.
Fourteen people died at Croke Park, including player Michael Hogan.
Three detainees died later that day at Dublin Castle.

overview.text: The Klondike Gold Rush began with an 1896 gold discovery near the Klondike River in what is now Canada’s Yukon. News spread widely in 1897, drawing prospectors north in hopes of finding claims. Many traveled through the Alaskan ports of Skagway and Dyea, crossed the Chilkoot or White Pass, and continued by boat toward Dawson City and the goldfields. The difficult journeys and boomtown growth transformed the region, while Indigenous communities faced disruption to lands and established trade routes. Many prospectors returned without wealth, and the rush declined quickly after its peak in 1898. The goldfields were in the Yukon, not Alaska.

key_facts.text: Gold was found near the Klondike River in the Yukon in August 1896.
The wider stampede followed news of the discovery in 1897.
Skagway and Dyea were Alaskan gateways to the Chilkoot and White Pass routes.
Prospectors traveled onward by river toward Dawson City.
The rush disrupted Indigenous communities and long-used Tlingit trade routes.

overview.text: The March on Rome was an October 1922 show of force by Italian Fascists that brought Benito Mussolini to the premiership. Armed supporters known as Blackshirts mobilized as they demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Luigi Facta; Mussolini himself stayed in Milan during the march. Facta sought emergency military measures, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to approve them and instead invited Mussolini to form a government. Mussolini initially led a coalition, then dismantled parliamentary democracy over the following years. The episode shows how Fascist violence and political pressure combined with a decision by the monarchy; the march itself was not a straightforward battlefield conquest of Rome.

key_facts.text: The March on Rome was staged on October 27–28, 1922.
Mussolini stayed in Milan while Fascist Blackshirts marched.
King Victor Emmanuel III refused to countersign Facta’s martial-law order.
The king invited Mussolini to form a new government.
Mussolini first headed a coalition before establishing a dictatorship.
